title: Coordination and supplementation
description: Explore non-headed coordination, coordinators and linked items, layered and gapped structures, and supplements that sit apart from the clause.
example: The guests and indeed most of the family stayed late, but the band had already packed up.

intro: Say *Kim and Pat speak excellent French* and the subject is two people joined on equal footing, neither leaning on the other the way a modifier leans on its head. Try *The tourists — most of them exhausted — got into the bus* and a phrase sits beside the clause, describing the tourists without being part of its grammar. English extends clauses in these two quite different ways, and the contrast between them runs through the chapter.

The first half works through coordination: what a coordinate is, how coordinators attach, and how binary and multiple, marked and unmarked, single and repeated marking differ. Layering, scope, joint readings and gapping follow, along with the surprisingly wide range of things that can be coordinated. The second half turns to supplements — appositives, parentheticals, relative clauses, dislocations — and to what detachment buys a speaker.

One distinction is worth carrying from the start. Coordinates are equal yet integrated: they form a unit together, and the coordinator travels with the coordinate it introduces. Supplements are related to an anchor but not integrated, held in place by prosody and discourse rather than by dependency. Equality and attachment are separate questions, and keeping them apart prevents most of the usual confusions.

blocks.text: Say *Kim and Pat speak excellent French* and the subject is not one person but two, joined on equal terms. Neither name governs the other; remove either and a subject remains. Now try *He can see you this afternoon or on Tuesday*, where the alternatives are not even the same kind of phrase. English lets such things stand side by side, and the result belongs to neither category: it is an NP/PP-coordination, a construction in its own right.

Nothing inside it acts as a centre of gravity. *Kim’s father* is a phrase about the father, and the possessor merely locates him; *Kim and Pat* is not about either name in that way. That is what non-headed means, and it is why the pair cannot be filed as an NP with two heads. The whole is a coordination of NPs, and the category of the whole is the coordination itself.

Reverse the names and the structure survives: *Pat and Kim* is the same kind of subject. Either name can often stand for the pair, as when *Kim and Pat* gives way to *they*. Neither test is a law, though. *Kim and Pat are a happy couple* will not accept one name in place of the pair, because the couple is precisely what the predicate is about — a reminder that equal status does not mean interchangeable meaning.

check.prompt: Why is Kim and Pat not simply an NP?

options.text: It is a non-headed NP-coordination, not an NP with one head.
options.feedback: The coordinates are equal and the whole has a coordination category.

blocks.text: Listen to where the coordinator sits. In *Kim and Pat* the natural break comes before *and*, not after it, and the same grouping shows up when the phrase moves: *And Pat* travels with its coordinator attached, while *Pat* is what remains once the linking material is stripped away. Hence the two labels. The expanded coordinate includes coordinator and modifiers; the bare coordinate is the core that is left.

Three observations point the same way. The second coordinate shifts position together with its coordinator; coordinators can open a sentence, as in *And so did her mother*; and the prosodic break falls before the coordinator rather than after it. Each is small on its own. Together they make it hard to treat *and* as a free-standing hinge between two equals.

Modifiers can expand a coordinate just as coordinators do. *He offended the guests and indeed his family too* dresses its second coordinate in *and*, *indeed* and *too*, so the unit set against *the guests* is larger than the noun phrase *his family* at its core. Equality of status survives the extra clothing: there are still two coordinates, and one of them simply wears more.

blocks.text: Count the coordinates and a first contrast appears. *Kim wrote a letter and Ed watched TV* has two, one clause on each side of the coordinator. *She wants to live in Sydney, London, or Paris* has three, and with three a new question arises: which of them carry a coordinator in front? Binary coordination never has to answer it. Multiple coordination always does.

Marking is the next variable. *He invited all his colleagues and all his students* announces its join; drop the *and* and the same list still coordinates, silently. A multiple coordination with a coordinator before the final coordinate only is simple-syndetic; one marked before every coordinate after the first is polysyndetic. The difference is audible in *Sydney, London, or Paris* set against *Sydney or London or Paris*.

Paired markers add a further layer. *Both ... and* and *either ... or* signal from the first coordinate that a second is coming; the initial word is a determinative, while *and* or *or* does the coordinating. Within a single layer of multiple coordination the medial coordinates must then be treated alike — all bare or all marked. Mix the two treatments and the structure has to be layered, which is the puzzle of the next section.

blocks.text: One coordination can sit inside another. *We should invite Kim and either Pat or Alex* invites Kim, then offers a choice between two others, so the *either ... or* pair is the second coordinate of a larger NP-coordination. Word order announces nothing. The brackets come from the sense.

*Egg and bacon or stew* can be read two ways, and the readings describe different dinners. Either the choice is between an egg-and-bacon dish and stew, or the choice is between egg and a bacon-or-stew dish. The words stay put; the structure shifts. Prosody and context tell a hearer which brackets to hear.

A single layer also demands consistency. *Kim, Tom and Pat, and your parents* leaves one medial coordinate bare and marks the other, so it cannot be a flat list of four; the comma before the last *and* signals a coordination nested inside a coordination. *Kim and Tom and Pat and your parents* can be either flat or layered, and punctuation or intonation decides which.

blocks.text: *I left the room and Pat followed me* joins two clauses, each with its own subject and predicate. *Kim and Pat speak excellent French* joins two names inside a single clause, which then supplies one predicate for both. Same coordinator, very different sizes of unit. Grammars keep the levels apart because the consequences differ.

At clause level each coordinate carries its own tense, subject and polarity. At subclausal level the coordinates share the clause’s remaining machinery, so agreement and scope have to be settled for the pair together. *Kim and Pat are a happy couple* shows how far that can go: the predicate does not apply to Kim and to Pat separately but to the two as a unit.

That last point opens a second distinction, between joint and distributed readings. *Kim and Pat are a happy couple* treats the pair as one entity; *Kim and Pat are tall* hands the property to each of them. The subject looks identical in both. The predicate chooses the reading.

blocks.text: Reverse a coordination and the grammar usually shrugs. *Kim and Pat* and *Pat and Kim* are equally good subjects, one reason coordinations look so unlike head-dependent phrases. This time the shrug is not universal. *They got married and had a baby* does not say what *They had a baby and got married* says, although the same two events are named.

Order carries meaning whenever the relation between coordinates is temporal, causal or rhetorical. *He got up and had breakfast* narrates a sequence; swap the clauses and the morning changes. *Hurry up or we’ll be late* offers no free choice at all — it threatens a consequence. The coordinates remain equal in status while the relation between them is anything but symmetrical.

There is a processing side as well. Complex or heavy coordinates tend to land late, where a reader or hearer can absorb them, and a contrastive coordinate may be held back for prominence. Syntax permits the reversal; discourse decides whether it earns its keep.

blocks.text: *And* joins, *or* divides — the schoolroom version, which logic sharpens: *and* needs both propositions true, *or* needs at least one. English then goes its own way. *He got up and had breakfast* is not a pair of independent facts but a sequence, and *Hurry up or we’ll be late* is a condition wearing the clothes of a choice.

Negation drags *and* and *or* into each other’s territory. De Morgan’s equivalences equate *not (A and B)* with *not A or not B*, and *not (A or B)* with *not A and not B*. Natural language adds a wrinkle: *not* can take scope over an entire coordination, so *He didn’t buy the report or the magazine* may deny both purchases or deny only the joint one, depending on how the coordination is bracketed.

One curious use of *and* builds meaning by repetition rather than conjunction. *Louder and louder*, *dozens and dozens*, *again and again* assert no pair of propositions; they convey increase, plurality or recurrence. The coordinator is doing aspectual work, and calling the result a simple conjunction misses what it is for.

sections.title: Both, either, neither, nor, and but

blocks.text: The paired markers come in fixed partnerships. *Both* looks ahead to *and*, *either* to *or*, *neither* to *nor*. In each pair the first word is a determinative announcing that another coordinate is on its way, and the coordinator arrives with the second coordinate to complete the job. Break the partnership — *both ... or*, *neither ... and* — and the sentence stumbles.

Negative pairing needs care. *Neither ... nor* is already negative, so *Neither Kim nor Pat came* needs no further *not*, and the pair can stand where clausal negation would otherwise go. *Nor* also works alone after a negative clause, continuing the negation as a connective: *He didn’t come, nor did she*.

Contrast and focus come from *but* and its relatives. *But* sets one coordinate against another or carves out an exception, as in *They allowed the others but not me*. *Not only* raises the first coordinate into prominence and usually calls for *but also* to finish the move: *She not only sings but also dances*, where the second coordinate, not the first, carries the surprise.

items.text: Both Kim and Pat agreed.

blocks.text: Not every linker is a coordinator, and the comparison-based ones show why. *As well as*, *rather than*, *more than* and *less than* join material while keeping their comparative sense. *She plays the piano as well as the violin* adds a second accomplishment; *rather than* sets one option aside instead of merely adding another to it.

Addition and inclusion have a small family of their own: *including*, *instead of*, *plus*, *besides*, *along with*. Their behaviour is not uniform. Some take noun phrase complements, some prefer gerund-participials, and some behave like prepositions that happen to sit between two items. Calling them all coordinators would flatten real differences.

Connective adverbs are the clearest impostors. *So*, *yet*, *however* and *therefore* link clauses or sentences in discourse, but they form no coordination: they are supplements or connective adjuncts, and they can move. *For*, *only* and resultative *so ... that* have specialised linking jobs of their own, each distinct from what a coordinator does.

sections.title: What can be coordinated with what

blocks.text: Coordination does not insist on matching categories. *He can see you this afternoon or on Tuesday* sets a noun phrase beside a prepositional phrase because both can say when. The result is an NP/PP-coordination, and what licenses it is the shared function, not a shared label.

The tolerance reaches further than one might expect. Grammaticised words coordinate when they share a role, as in *the before and after photographs* or *the up and down movement*; genitives coordinate in *Kim’s and Pat’s reports*; even clause types can be mismatched, as in *Come around six, or is that too early for you?*, where an imperative is followed by an interrogative.

Level matters throughout. The same string can be analysed as a coordination of words, phrases, clauses or whole sentences, and the choice changes what counts as agreeing, what falls within the scope of a modifier, and what the sentence commits its speaker to.

blocks.text: Some coordinations do not wear their structure on the surface. Expansion is the mildest case: a coordinate padded with modifiers, as in *The guests and indeed his family too*. Gapping cuts deeper. *Kim is an engineer and Pat a barrister* drops the verb from the second coordinate, and the missing *is* is recovered from the first: two predications, one verb.

Others coordinate sequences that are not phrases at all. *I gave $10 to Kim and $5 to Pat* pairs *$10 to Kim* with *$5 to Pat* — right-hand runs that never function as constituents elsewhere, hence the name right nonce-constituent coordination. Delayed right constituent coordination goes the other way, holding a shared phrase until both coordinates have passed: *I knew of but never mentioned my work*.

End-attachment coordination simply hangs the second coordinate on the end of the clause: *They had found Kim guilty, but not Pat*. What makes such patterns valuable is also what makes them tricky. A stretch of words that can be coordinated with a matching stretch is probably a constituent, so coordination probes clause structure; but nonce constituents show that the construction can also manufacture units for its own purposes.

blocks.text: *The tourists — most of them exhausted — got into the bus.* The clause is complete without the interruption, yet the interruption is not noise: *most of them exhausted* describes the tourists, and the dashes mark it off as something said beside the clause rather than inside it. That detached constituent is a supplement, and *the tourists* is its anchor.

Integration separates a supplement from a dependent. A dependent belongs to its head’s syntax — *the exhausted tourists* cannot lose *exhausted* without losing part of the noun phrase. A supplement hangs on by discourse and prosody instead. It may elaborate, comment, evaluate, attribute or identify, but it does so from outside the dependency structure of the clause.

Supplements come in many shapes, from NPs and adjective phrases through PPs to finite and non-finite clauses. The noun phrase in *My friend, a doctor* identifies its anchor; an adverb may instead evaluate the clause, and a relative clause may add a comment without restricting it. What they share is the comma, the dash or the parenthesis — and the freedom to be lifted out.

blocks.text: Function and form cross-cut in supplements. *My friend, a doctor, called* elaborates an anchor; *Fortunately, nobody was hurt* comments on a clause; *The report, according to Kim, was leaked* attributes a claim; *The report, which was leaked, caused a scandal* adds a relative clause. One detached position accommodates all four, and the punctuation carries much of the signal.

Appositives are the central case, because the supplement and its anchor name the same thing twice. *My friend, a doctor* characterises or identifies; either part could stand alone, and the comma tells the reader to take them together. Parentheticals comment rather than rename — *The plan, I think, will work* — while dislocations move an NP to the edge and leave a pronoun behind to hold its place: *Kim, I like her*.

It would be a mistake to file supplements as optional dependents. Optionality is not the issue; integration is. The same content can sit inside the clause or beside it, and the difference shows in syntax and in how the information is presented. *The exhausted tourists left* makes exhaustion part of who left; *The tourists, exhausted, left* offers it as an aside.

blocks.text: Coordination has long served as a probe for constituent structure. If a stretch of words can be coordinated with a matching stretch, it behaves like a unit, and units are what clauses are built from. The probe is powerful, but it is not mechanical: nonce constituents and end-attachment show that coordination can also create units which do not exist independently.

Scope ambiguity is where the machinery gets interesting. *Long poems and essays* can mean long poems and long essays, or long poems together with essays of any length; *new and second-hand books* can describe books that are new or second-hand, or a collection composed of two kinds. The words are identical and the structures are not, so prosody, context and the predicate must decide.

Nonce constituents complicate the picture further. *I gave $10 to Kim and $5 to Pat* coordinates right-hand sequences that are not ordinary phrases; delayed right constituent coordination holds the shared phrase until after both coordinates, as in *I knew of but never mentioned my work*; end-attachment adds the second coordinate at the end, as in *They had found Kim guilty, but not Pat*.

The analyst therefore faces three questions rather than one. What are the coordinates? What material do they share? What scope does the coordination have? A sentence may be grammatical under more than one answer, and the work lies in seeing which answers the evidence actually supports.

blocks.text: *Kim, I like her.* The name sits outside the clause, and the pronoun inside does the grammatical work. Move the name to the other end and the mirror image appears: *I like her, Kim*. In the first, left dislocation, the NP opens the utterance; in the second, right dislocation, it arrives after the clause as an afterthought or clarification.

Parentheticals are close relatives with a different job. *The plan, I think, will work* and *The report, according to Kim, was leaked* interrupt or follow the clause in order to comment on it, hedge it or attribute it. They carry modal, evidential or attributive meaning, and they are not dependents of the verb.

What unites the two is detachment. Dislocation leaves a pronoun to fill the gap; parentheticals leave the clause intact and add a voice beside it. In both cases the relation to the anchor runs through discourse and prosody rather than through head-dependent syntax.

Take *Kim, I like her*: *Kim* is not the object of *like*; *her* is, and the verb takes its object from the pronoun. *The plan, I think, will work* is different: *I think* comments on the clause without making *I* the subject of *work*. Each piece keeps its own structure.

blocks.text: Two coordinates, no head, equal status: that is the shape coordination keeps. The coordinates may be two or many, marked or unmarked, linked by a single final coordinator or by one before every coordinate after the first, plain or paired with a correlative. The coordinator travels with the coordinate that follows it, and a coordinate may be bare or dressed up with modifiers.

The structures can nest. Coordinations layer inside one another, join clauses or smaller units, take joint or distributed readings, and survive gapping and the other non-basic patterns. Categories need not match so long as functions do. *And* and *or* carry logical and asymmetric senses; *both/either*, *neither/nor*, *but*, *not only* and the comparison-based linkers extend the inventory.

Supplementation works from the other direction. A supplement is detached from its anchor — an appositive, a parenthetical, a relative clause, an evaluation or a dislocation — and relates to it through discourse and prosody. Coordination integrates equals; supplementation leaves a companion standing beside the clause.

blocks.title: A coordination checklist
blocks.text: Identify the coordinates and the coordinator. Decide whether the coordination is binary or multiple, syndetic or asyndetic. Check for layering, gapping or nonce constituents. Then ask whether the relation is clausal or subclausal, joint or distributed, and whether a supplement rather than a coordination is involved.

check.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes coordination from supplementation?

options.text: Coordination joins equal coordinates; supplementation relates a detached expression to an anchor.
options.feedback: Coordination is non-headed but integrated; supplementation is detached.

options.text: Coordination always has two coordinates; supplementation always has three.
Supplements are dependents of a head.

worked: Take *The guests and indeed most of the family stayed late, but the band had already packed up*. The first coordination is *The guests and indeed most of the family*, an NP-coordination functioning as subject. The second coordinate is expanded by *indeed*, and the whole coordination is joined by *but* to the clause *the band had already packed up*.

The example contains both subclausal and clausal coordination: the NP-coordination is the subject of the first clause, and the two clauses are coordinated by *but*. The coordinator belongs with the following coordinate in each case, and the second coordinate of the subject is expanded by a modifier.
application: Identify the coordinates and the coordinator. Check whether the coordination is binary or multiple, syndetic or asyndetic. If multiple, decide whether it is simple-syndetic or polysyndetic, and check for correlative markers.

Look for layering, gapping, nonce constituents and end-attachment. Then decide whether the coordination is clausal or subclausal, joint or distributed. The same sequence may have more than one structure, so use prosody and meaning to resolve the ambiguity.

For supplementation, identify the anchor and the supplement. Check whether the supplement is an appositive, parenthetical, relative clause, evaluation or dislocation. Supplements are detached, so do not analyse them as ordinary dependents.
reveal: In *The guests and indeed most of the family stayed late, but the band had already packed up*, the subject is an NP-coordination of *the guests* and *indeed most of the family*. *But* coordinates that clause with *the band had already packed up*. The second subject coordinate is expanded by *indeed*.
recap: Coordination is non-headed and joins equal coordinates. It can be binary or multiple, syndetic or asyndetic, simple-syndetic or polysyndetic, correlative or non-correlative. Coordinators belong with the following coordinate, and coordinates can be bare or expanded.

Layering, gapping and nonce constituents show that coordination can be structurally complex. Supplementation relates a detached expression to an anchor and includes appositives, parentheticals, relative clauses and dislocations.
